question: Which antibiotics are safe to use in kidney transplant patients with impaired graft function (reduced eGFR) requiring dose adjustment?

must_have: Names specific commonly used antibiotics with their renal handling (e.g. ceftriaxone usually needs no renal dose adjustment; cefepime requires dose reduction at reduced CrCl with neurotoxicity risk if unadjusted; amoxicillin/amoxicillin-clavulanate need adjustment in severe impairment; TMP-SMX needs dose reduction and potassium monitoring)
Flags aminoglycosides (gentamicin/amikacin/tobramycin) as nephrotoxic and NOT a renal-safe default for a vulnerable graft even where resistance data favor their coverage
Surfaces the immunosuppressant interaction axis: macrolides such as clarithromycin/erythromycin raise tacrolimus/cyclosporine levels (CYP3A) requiring trough monitoring
Every drug-specific claim is supported by evidence about THAT drug or class — no citations from unrelated (non-antibiotic) drug labels presented as antibiotic evidence
nice_to_have: Distinguishes eGFR from CrCl thresholds used on labels
Notes vancomycin needs individualized dosing with level monitoring
Keeps resistance-pattern findings (e.g. graft pyelonephritis empiric coverage) clearly separate from safety/dosing guidance

answer:
## Bottom line
Direct data on antibiotic renal dosing specifically in kidney transplant recipients (KTR) are limited to acute graft pyelonephritis (AGPN): aminoglycosides (e.g., amikacin) and carbapenems are the only classes with resistance rates under 10% in AGPN, and a combination regimen including amikacin has been suggested as an appropriate empirical strategy — but aminoglycosides are themselves [[K]]nephrotoxic and require renal dose adjustment[[/K]] [1]. Beyond this, the evidence establishes only the general nephrology principle that renally-cleared drugs, including many antibiotics, must have doses reduced in proportion to reduced clearance rather than being categorically avoided [2][13][14].

## Efficacy
- In kidney transplant recipients with acute graft pyelonephritis (AGPN), [[F]]aminoglycosides and carbapenems were the only antimicrobial classes with resistance rates <10%[[/F]], and none of the antibiotics typically recommended for empirical UTI treatment achieved <10% resistance against AGPN, so none should be used as monotherapy; a combination therapy including amikacin was suggested as an appropriate strategy [1].
- In healthcare-associated infections in KTR, cefepime or a piperacillin-tazobactam combination are more often used, though the findings do not report efficacy/resistance figures for these two agents specifically [12].
- No findings report comparative efficacy (cure rates, resistance %, outcome timepoints) for other antibiotic classes in KTR with reduced eGFR.

## Safety & adverse effects
- Aminoglycosides (e.g., amikacin), while effective against AGPN pathogens, [[F]]carry nephrotoxicity risk and require renal dose adjustment[[/F]] — a particular concern in patients who already have impaired graft function [1].
- General nephrology guidance: in renal impairment, drug dose should be decreased "equivalently to the calculated reduction of drug clearance" [2], because renally cleared drugs have altered effects when clearance is reduced [13].
- In critically ill patients with acute kidney injury, especially those on renal replacement therapy, careful antimicrobial dose management is essential, since AKI itself alters pharmacokinetics and extracorporeal removal during renal replacement therapy can be clinically significant, risking underdosing, treatment failure, or resistance if not accounted for [3].

## Population
- The AGPN/resistance findings apply specifically to [[K]]kidney transplant recipients with acute graft pyelonephritis[[/K]], the most frequent infectious complication in this population [11], and to UTI more broadly, the most common infection after transplantation, associated with impaired allograft function [10].
- The healthcare-associated infection finding on cefepime/piperacillin-tazobactam applies to KTR with HCA infections specifically [12].
- The general dose-adjustment principles [2][13][14] apply broadly to patients with acute or chronic kidney disease/renal impairment, not specifically to transplant recipients, and are not antibiotic-specific.
- The critical-illness/AKI-RRT dosing findings [3] apply to critically ill patients with acute kidney injury, particularly those requiring renal replacement therapy — a population that may overlap with, but is not limited to, kidney transplant recipients with reduced eGFR.

## Evidence quality
- [[R]]The AGPN resistance/treatment-strategy findings [1][11][12] derive from a single observational study on empirical antibiotic optimization in transplant recipients — this reflects real-world resistance patterns in a defined population but is not a randomized comparison of dosing regimens or graded guideline recommendation.[[/R]]
- The renal dose-adjustment principles [2][13][14] come from general nephrology/pharmacology reference sources (StatPearls, drug-dosing review) describing accepted standard practice, not from antibiotic-specific trials.
- The AKI/critical-illness dosing guidance [3] is a narrative guide on antimicrobial pharmacokinetics in critical illness/renal replacement therapy, not a randomized trial with reported clinical outcomes.
- No systematic review, guideline, or randomized trial specifically addressing antibiotic dose adjustment by eGFR level in kidney transplant recipients is present in these findings.

## Not addressed
The findings do not provide a list of specific antibiotics deemed "safe" with defined dose-adjustment regimens by eGFR threshold in kidney transplant recipients; they also lack specific dosing figures (mg, interval changes) for any antibiotic in this population, and do not report efficacy/safety outcomes for cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam themselves.

claims.text: That same study found aminoglycosides and carbapenems were the only antimicrobial classes with resistance rates under 10% in kidney transplant recipients with acute graft pyelonephritis, and suggested a combination including amikacin (an aminoglycoside) as an appropriate empirical strategy — though aminoglycosides themselves carry nephrotoxicity risk and require renal dose adjustment.
claims.quote:
The only antimicrobials with resistance rates < 10 % were aminoglycosides and carbapenems.

Conclusion: None of the antibiotics recommended in empirical treatment in UTIs has shown a resistance rate of less than 10% with regard to AGPN. Therefore, none of them should be used as monotherapy. A combination therapy including amikacin could be an appropriate strategy in this setting.
claims.title: Toward an optimization of empirical antibiotic therapy in acute graft pyelonephritis: A retrospective multicenter study - PubMed

claims.text: General nephrology guidance (StatPearls) establishes that in patients with reduced kidney function, renally-cleared drugs (which includes many antibiotics) require dose reduction proportional to the decrease in drug clearance, rather than being categorically avoided.
claims.quote: In summary, the medication dose should be decreased equivalently to the calculated reduction of drug clearance.
claims.title: Renal Failure Drug Dose Adjustments - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf (2024)

claims.text: For critically ill patients with acute kidney injury, especially those requiring renal replacement therapy, careful antimicrobial dosing adjustment is essential, as extracorporeal removal during renal replacement therapy can be clinically significant and risks underdosing/treatment failure or resistance if not accounted for.
claims.quote: A careful management of antimicrobials is essential in the critically ill with acute kidney injury, especially if renal replacement therapy is required. Acute kidney injury may lead per se to clinically significant modifications of drugs’ pharmacokinetic parameters, and the need for renal replacement therapy represents a further variable that should be considered to avoid inappropriate antimicrobial therapy.
claims.title: A Guide to Understanding Antimicrobial Drug Dosing in Critically Ill Patients on Renal Replacement Therapy
